name: Determining When at Least One of the Three Boolean Variables is False
description: Construct a program that determines whether at least one of the three boolean variables is False based on the inputs that it receives from the user.
code:
#Step 1: Read the user input for the value of the first boolean variable (variable a)
text = input("Enter 1 if the value of the first boolean variable (variable a) is True, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 2: Determine whether the value of the first boolean variable (variable a) is True 
if input_num == 1 :
    a = True
else:
    a = False
#Step 3: Read the user input for the value of the second boolean variable (variable b)
text = input("Enter 1 if the value of the second boolean variable (variable b) is True, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 4: Determine whether the value of the second boolean variable (variable b) is True 
if input_num == 1 :
    b = True
else:
    b = False
#Step 5: Read the user input for the value of the third boolean variable (variable c)
text = input("Enter 1 if the value of the third boolean variable (variable c) is True, otherwise enter 0:")
input_num = int(text)
#Step 6: Determine whether the value of the third boolean variable (variable c) is True 
if input_num == 1 :
    c = True
else:
    c = False
#Step 7: Write the boolean expression to determine whether at least one of the three boolean variables is False
result = not (a and b and c)
#Step 8: Print the result
if result == True :
    print("Yes! At least one of the three boolean variables is False.")
else:
    print("No! None of the boolean variables are False.")

26.content: result = not (a and b and c)
commentList: Purpose: This line computes whether at least one of the three boolean variables is False and stores that answer in the variable result so you can use it later to decide what to print.

Syntax and meaning: You assign to result the value of not (a and b and c). The expression (a and b and c) is True only when all three variables are True; applying not flips that value, so result becomes True when at least one variable is False.

How it works in practice: If a, b, and c are all True then (a and b and c) is True and result becomes False; if any one (or more) of a, b, c is False then (a and b and c) is False and result becomes True — that matches the problem requirement.

Common misconception and error to avoid: Do not write not a and b and c if you mean to negate the whole conjunction — that expression is parsed differently and applies not only to the whole group. Using parentheses as shown makes your intent clear and avoids precedence confusion.

Best practice: Make sure a, b, and c are actual booleans before this line. For readability you might also use result = not all([a, b, c]) or choose a more descriptive name like at_least_one_false to make the code clearer to you and others.

distractors.code: result = (not a) and (not b) and (not c)
distractors.description: You might choose this because it looks like you negated every variable to check for falseness. Step by step: this expression is True only when a is False AND b is False AND c is False. If even one variable is True, the whole expression becomes False. A common reason you'd pick this is believing that negating each variable and joining with AND finds a single False value, but instead it demands that every variable be False. Replacing the original line with this makes the program report 'Yes' only when all three inputs are 0; in cases where one or two variables are False (but not all three), the program will incorrectly report 'No'. The key mistake here is treating 'at least one is False' as if it required 'all are False.'

distractors.code: result = a or b or c
distractors.description: You might pick this because 'or' often reads as 'at least one', so you could think 'a or b or c' checks 'at least one' of something. But this expression is True when at least one variable is True, not when at least one is False. If you use this line, the program will print 'Yes! At least one of the three boolean variables is False.' whenever any input was 1 — which is the opposite of what you want. For example, if all three inputs are 1, this line makes result True and the program prints 'Yes', even though there are no False values. The error is confusing what property (truth vs falsity) the OR is testing.

distractors.code: result = not (a or b or c)
distractors.description: You might choose this because negating the group 'a or b or c' seems like a way to check for falseness. Step by step: this expression is True only when a, b, and c are all False (because a or b or c must be False for the negation to be True). If one variable is False but another is True, 'a or b or c' is True and the negation is False. Using this line makes the program report 'Yes' only when every input is 0; in most other situations where at least one variable is False (but not all), the program will incorrectly report 'No'. The underlying mistake is treating 'at least one is False' as if it meant 'none are True.'

distractors.code: result = a and b and c
distractors.description: This distractor uses the logical AND operator across all three variables: result = a and b and c. A student might pick this thinking that testing whether all three are true detects whether at least one is false. However, this expression is True only when all three variables are True, directly inverting the requirement to detect when at least one variable is False.
